 Anua brings KPop Demon Hunters into Olive Young's Seoul beauty house
 Anua brought KPop Demon Hunters to a themed Olive Young pop-up in Seoul, connecting licensed skincare with an in-store fan experience.
 Zoe Park 
 25 Oct 2026 
 • 3 min read

 ↓ 
 Netflix's KPop Demon Hunters moved into a new kind of beauty setting in Seoul this October. Korean skincare brand Anua brought its licensed products to a themed Hunters Beauty House at Olive Young N Seongsu, inviting visitors into a retail environment modeled on the fictional group's makeup room.
 The activation ran October 1-12, 2026, according to a Korean event listing and an October 1 event announcement. Rather than presenting a new partnership, it offered a physical chapter in Anua's existing year-long collaboration with Netflix.
 A makeup-room concept becomes a retail pop-up
 Anua taps KPop Demon Hunters fandom with year-long skincare collaboration Anua’s latest campaign turns skincare into a cultural experience for K-pop and animation fans. ContentGrip Hunters Beauty House event announcement image. The Popply event listing placed Hunters Beauty House at Olive Young N Seongsu, 13 Yeonmujang 7-gil, in Seoul's Seongdong district. The pop-up operated from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. during its October 1-12 run.
 Its pitch was straightforward: visitors were invited into the hunters' makeup room. The listing highlighted limited-edition Anua x KPop Demon Hunters spot patches and Golden Wrapping mask packs, sold at the venue during the activation period. An October 1 event announcement corroborated the venue and dates.
 The available sources do not establish visitor numbers, sell-through, or whether the activation changed purchase behavior. Those results should not be inferred from the event's design.
 How the Seoul event extends Anua's Netflix partnership
 This was not the beginning of the Anua partnership. Netflix previously described a year-long skincare collaboration, connecting the animated film's protective mythology with products including Honmoon-themed masks, sunscreens and acne patches.
 The Seongsu activation moved that product story into a specific place. A fan could encounter the branded skincare inside a setting built around the fictional performers, rather than only seeing character imagery on a product listing. That distinction matters: physical retail can turn entertainment licensing into a visitable experience.
 ContentGrip has covered the broader Anua collaboration , including its product lineup and fandom strategy. Hunters Beauty House offers a narrower view of how the same licensing program can be expressed through a temporary retail destination.
 Why Olive Young N Seongsu is part of the story
 The venue is more than a backdrop. By placing the activation inside a beauty retailer, Anua connected a fantasy-inspired makeup-room concept with a real point of product discovery.
 That combination gives a pop-up two jobs. It can create an experience recognizable to people familiar with the film, while keeping the skincare products close to a shopping context. The event listing's focus on limited-edition patches and masks reinforces that relationship between themed participation and retail merchandise.
 The publicly available evidence does not show whether visitors purchased products or whether Olive Young benefited commercially. The observable strategy is the blending of a licensed entertainment world with an existing beauty retail environment.
 What marketers can learn from Hunters Beauty House
 The Seoul pop-up illustrates how a licensing program can gain another chapter without pretending every activation is a brand-new collaboration.
 1. Make the fiction tangible. A makeup-room setting provides a recognizable bridge from the film's characters to beauty products.
 2. Keep the product in view. The listed spot patches and masks gave the experience a concrete retail connection, rather than making it solely a photo opportunity.
 3. Use time limits carefully. A 12-day event creates a defined window for discovery, but duration alone is not evidence of demand or success.
 4. Separate engagement design from outcomes. Event images and themed spaces demonstrate creative execution. Claims about sales, footfall and earned media require separate evidence.
 The larger lesson is that fandom partnerships can travel across formats. A product collection, a campaign film and a temporary shop may all express the same intellectual property in different ways.
 For Anua, Hunters Beauty House was a location-specific extension of its Netflix tie-in, not proof of a new wave of commercial growth. Its value as a marketing case lies in the mechanics that can be observed: a familiar entertainment world, a fitting retail venue and products designed to connect the two.
